passage_changes.passage: Ceuta is a small Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa. It is bordered on its land side by a neighbouring state, and a strong fence separates the enclave from that country. Many of those who arrive there are seeking work, education or a better life, while others are fleeing conflict or persecution in their home countries. Tensions over a distant territory add another layer to the story. Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony, has been the subject of a long dispute involving neighbouring countries and groups seeking self-determination. Changes in the relations between Spain and its neighbours have, at different times, affected how many people reach the enclave. Ceuta's story shows how geography and politics can combine. A place that is small on the map can become a major point of diplomacy when large numbers of people try to cross into it. Resolving such moments usually depends on cooperation between governments, as well as on the legal rules that protect people who seek safety. Such episodes also test how well the rules protecting people who seek safety are applied in practice.

India imports a large part of the crude oil and natural gas it uses, and policymakers have long wanted more of this supply to come from within the country. Much of the unexplored potential lies beneath the sea, in deep and far-off waters where drilling is costly and technically demanding. Companies hesitate to commit money to such projects because results can take years to arrive. At the same time, the fields that already produce oil and gas do not stay productive forever. Their output falls every year as the reservoirs age, so new discoveries are needed just to keep production steady.

The Samudra Manthan Scheme is the government's response to this problem. It is built around several linked streams of work. Some streams focus on locating resources and on drilling in difficult waters. Others focus on shared facilities that can move produced oil and gas, on building a domestic base of manufacturing and services, and on developing skills and technology. The plan also sets a clear quantity goal, aiming to add a large volume of reserves and to raise annual domestic output. Taken together, the scheme hopes to reduce risk for investors, strengthen national capability, and make India less reliant on imported energy in the years ahead.

Sarnath, a Buddhist site in Uttar Pradesh, has recently been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The inscription was made at a meeting of the World Heritage Committee, and it raised the total number of such sites in India. Sarnath holds a special place in Buddhist history because Gautama Buddha gave his first teaching there after attaining enlightenment at Bodhgaya. The event marks the beginning of the Buddhist monastic community, known as the Sangha, and it is linked with the Noble Eightfold Path. The site was known in earlier times by several names, and it is visited today for its monuments. Visitors see the Chaukhandi, Dhamekh and Dharmarajika stupas, a vihara and the Ashokan Pillar. Many of these structures are linked with episodes from the Buddha's life or with rulers of the past. Sarnath is also counted among the principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites. India has many heritage sites of different kinds, grouped as cultural, natural and mixed. Each category holds its own set of monuments, and together they show how varied the country's heritage is. The process of recognition involves assessment by expert bodies before the final decision is taken by the committee. Such a listing is a major achievement for any country, because it brings the monument to the attention of the whole world.

The 17th round of talks under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification recently concluded in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia. The meeting coincided with a United Nations observance that draws attention to pastoral communities and the management of rangelands, which are grasslands and open lands used for grazing. The emphasis on pastoral communities reflects how directly their livelihoods depend on the condition of the land. Land degradation was a central concern. It is described as a serious threat to ecosystems, farming, the availability of water and the economic stability of many regions. The crisis affects a large share of the world's land, and delegates argued that restoring whole landscapes is more effective than scattered, isolated projects. Mongolia used the platform to explain the severity of its own problem, and it has a national campaign to plant trees over the coming years. Several countries also promoted nature-based solutions and ecosystem restoration as part of national development planning. The convention itself is a legally binding framework dealing with desertification, land degradation and drought, and its work connects closely with climate and biodiversity agreements. Its broader aim is sustainable land management, so that land continues to support people and nature.

Glaw Lake, a lake in the Eastern Himalayas, has recently gained recognition as a wetland of global importance. It lies in Arunachal Pradesh, and its waters are fresh rather than salty. The lake sits within a protected area. The recognition came under the Ramsar Convention, the intergovernmental treaty on wetlands. It is the only international treaty that addresses one specific ecosystem. Under this treaty, wetlands of international importance are declared as Ramsar sites. The term wetland is broad. It describes any area of land covered by water, whether that water is salt, fresh or somewhere in between, and whether it is present seasonally or permanently. Wetland types include rivers, swamps, wet grasslands, peatlands, deltas and tidal flats, as well as mangroves and coral reefs. The treaty has been in force for decades and has many member states. Glaw Lake's recognition is an example of a wider expansion of India's protected wetlands network. India has steadily added sites to its Ramsar network over the years. India also runs a National Wetland Conservation Program, implemented through state authorities. Government schemes also support this work. One scheme focuses on the optimal use of wetlands, and its aims include enhancing biodiversity, carbon stock and income for local communities. Another focus is moving from high-volume tourism to nature tourism at ecologically sensitive wetlands.

Scotland is set to host the Commonwealth Games for the fourth time, after earlier editions in Edinburgh and Glasgow. The 2026 edition was staged in Glasgow and brought together athletes from the nations and territories of the Commonwealth. The Games are organised by the Commonwealth Games Federation, and the event has a long history that began with a sporting competition held in London in 1911. Glasgow had hosted the event once before, in 2014, so the city has welcomed the Games previously.

The programme for 2026 covered a wide range of disciplines, including athletics, swimming, cycling, weightlifting, boxing and judo. Teams from many countries took part, although not every nation entered every discipline. India's contingent included para athletes, and its medal count was reported at the close of the event. Indian women boxers were among the standout performers of the event, and several of them won gold medals.

At the closing ceremony, India's flag was carried by boxer Jaismine Lamboria, who had won a gold medal in the women's 57 kg category. Medal tallies are widely reported, and they are a common way to compare how countries performed across the event.

The Dirac Medal is an annual award that honours the legacy of the renowned physicist Paul Dirac. Dirac is remembered as one of the founders of modern quantum mechanics, and the medal carries his name. In 2026, the medal was awarded to the physicist Deepak Dhar, who shared the honour with three other physicists. The recognition was given for pioneering work in statistical mechanics, the field in which their research lies. Each recipient of the award receives a medal, which marks the honour in a tangible form. The award is given every year, and the 2026 medal is the latest of these presentations. Readers preparing for competitive examinations should keep the winners, the field of the work and the namesake of the award together while revising. Knowing the namesake links the medal to the history of quantum mechanics, and knowing the field helps in identifying the 2026 work. This item appears in the AILET Corner of the August 2026 current affairs section. A short written summary, with each detail on its own line, makes these facts easier to recall before an examination. Each of the details above is part of the same award, so revising them together helps in keeping the item clear in memory.

International law on refugees and trafficking is built from several separate agreements rather than one document. Some agreements focus on organised crime and on protecting people, especially women and children, from being exploited. Others define who counts as a refugee, what rights that person should have, and why a refugee must not be sent back to a place of danger. Still other treaties cover civil and political rights, and they include protections against cruel treatment when a person is returned to their home country. The framework also reaches children, whose welfare in conflict and displacement is addressed by a separate treaty on their rights. The Global Compact on Refugees (2018) offers a framework to support refugees and host countries. The Global Refugee Forum is held every four years to address challenges faced by refugees and host communities. India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol. Each agreement was written for a different purpose, so their scope and obligations vary. Overall, the system combines criminal law, human rights and humanitarian commitments into one broad structure.

The selection of the UN Secretary-General combines written rules with long-standing custom. The founding Charter explains how the post is filled, but it does not set a limit on how long the holder may serve. Over time, a standard length of office has developed through practice, and the holder is normally allowed to seek a further term, although this rests on custom rather than written rules. The Security Council plays the decisive role in the process. The Council has fifteen members, and each one holds a single vote, so its recommendation reflects collective judgment rather than the preference of one state. When the Council settles on a candidate, its recommendation passes to the wider membership of the United Nations, which makes the formal appointment. Even though that wider body could decide by a simple majority, appointments have usually been made without a vote, through agreement or general approval. The choice is also shaped by an unwritten expectation that the post should move between different parts of the world. This expectation is meant to give every region a fair chance of representation at the top of the organisation. Candidates are expected to present their experience and their vision for the organisation before member states. The practice reflects an effort to balance representation across the world.

Offshore hydrocarbon exploration needs large sums of public money before any oil or gas reaches the market. Surveys of the seabed, test drilling in deep water and the construction of shared facilities all require heavy spending. The government has therefore set aside a fixed amount for the scheme for a defined period. The money is divided among several heads, covering drilling, data collection, common infrastructure and manufacturing zones. Some of these heads are large and others are small, reflecting their different roles.

The government has also chosen to share part of the cost of drilling with companies that take part. This is meant to lower the financial risk that makes private firms hesitant about offshore work. The sharing applies only to eligible drilling costs. Officials expect that the combination of public allocations and shared risk will encourage firms to commit capital and bring technology to difficult frontier areas. The scheme's funding is therefore a central feature of its design.

Drought is one of the harder environmental problems to manage. For a long time, the usual response has been relief once the harm is done. A newer approach asks governments to look at how exposed they are before the damage occurs. To support this, a comprehensive technical instrument was introduced to help countries judge how prepared they are for drought. It draws on modern data-analysis tools, studies the vulnerability of communities and maps the risks they face. Money is the other side of the problem. Public funds can play a catalytic role, bringing in private and institutional investors to finance water security, climate-resilient farming and land restoration. A fresh pool of finance announced at the recent conference was meant for restoring land and building drought resilience in vulnerable countries. Discussions about a binding global instrument for drought form part of the wider debate. Land and water are closely linked. Overall, drought is best understood as a problem of preparation and investment, not only of emergency response.

Tiger reserves are protected areas that receive a special status so that tigers can breed, move and live without constant disturbance. In India, these areas are created under a national programme that gives them legal backing and dedicated management. Any change to a reserve's boundaries needs careful approval, because the rules are meant to protect the animals within them. Officials therefore treat reserve notification as a formal process, not a routine administrative step. Tiger reserves vary greatly in size, from Bor (Maharashtra), the smallest, to Nagarjunsagar Srisailam, the largest. Their tiger numbers are estimated through a periodic count carried out by official agencies with the help of research institutes. Counting takes place in fixed cycles, so that results from different years can be compared. Some states have many reserves while others have only a few. Software-based monitoring systems help managers track conditions in these reserves and respond to threats. Local communities also play a role, because conservation in and around forests depends on people living alongside wildlife. The scale of this work is large, and even small changes in reserve boundaries can affect many animals. Together, these features explain why tiger reserves remain central to the country's conservation strategy.

The idea of a sporting contest across the Commonwealth is older than the Games themselves. It can be traced to an event held in London in 1911, which formed part of a Festival of Empire organised during the coronation celebrations of King George V. The first edition of the Games was held in 1930 in a Canadian city, and the concept is credited to a sportswriter from the same country. The event was generally held once every four years, although the editions scheduled for 1942 and 1946 did not take place.

Over the decades the event has carried several different titles, and its name has changed more than once. Today the Games are organised by the Commonwealth Games Federation. India has hosted the Games, and its best performance at the Games, with 101 medals, came at that edition.

A centenary edition of the Games is planned for India in a future year, which will mark one hundred years since the first Games. India's first participation came decades before it hosted the Games, showing a long link with the event. The Games are a multi-sport event in which athletes from many nations compete for medals across a range of sports.

facts.title: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 and the 2026 Bill
facts.summary: The 1971 Act makes insult to the National Flag and Constitution, and preventing the singing of the National Anthem, punishable offences. A Bill proposes to bring Vande Mataram under similar statutory protection. The Bill proposes imprisonment up to 3 years, fine or both for intentionally insulting the song.
facts: Section 2 prohibits intentional insult to or disrespect for the National Flag and Constitution.
Examples under Section 2 include burning, defacing, desecrating or showing disrespect.
Section 3 prohibits intentionally preventing the singing of the National Anthem.
Section 3 also prohibits causing disturbance to an assembly during its singing.
Sections 2 and 3 each carry up to 3 years' imprisonment, fine or both.
Section 3A was inserted through the 2003 Amendment.
Section 3A prescribes a minimum 1 year imprisonment for second and subsequent convictions under Sections 2 or 3.
The Bill seeks to extend statutory protection to Vande Mataram, similar to that for the National Anthem.
Under the Bill, intentionally insulting Vande Mataram would be punishable.
Proposed Bill punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years, fine or both.

facts.title: Glaw Lake and India's Ramsar Network
facts.summary: Glaw Lake, a pristine freshwater lake in the Eastern Himalayas region of Arunachal Pradesh, became India's 101st Ramsar Site. It lies in the protected area of Kamlang Tiger Reserve and Wildlife Sanctuary.
facts: Glaw Lake became India's 101st Ramsar Site
Location: Arunachal Pradesh; region: Eastern Himalayas
Type: pristine freshwater lake
Protected area: Kamlang Tiger Reserve and Wildlife Sanctuary
Largest Indian Ramsar site: Sunderbans, West Bengal
Smallest Indian Ramsar site: Vembannur Wetland Complex, Tamil Nadu
Maximum Ramsar sites in one state: Tamil Nadu (14)
Named Indian Ramsar sites: Chilika, Keoladeo, Harike, Loktak and Wular

facts.title: India's medal performance at Glasgow 2026
facts.summary: India won 39 medals and finished 4th on the medal tally, behind Australia, England and Canada. This was fewer than the 61 medals India won at Birmingham 2022. The booklet links the lower count to a reduced contingent and to the absence of several traditional medal-producing disciplines.
facts: India's total: 39 medals
Medal tally position: 4th, behind Australia, England and Canada
India won 61 medals at Birmingham 2022
Boxing was India's best sport: 10 medals (7 gold, 3 silver)
Highest-ever boxing gold tally by India at the Commonwealth Games
Reduced contingent cited as a reason for the lower count
Absence of traditional medal-producing disciplines, including Shooting, Wrestling, Badminton, Hockey and Table Tennis
India did not field teams in 3x3 Basketball or Netball

facts.title: Notable Indian achievements
facts.summary: Several Indian athletes produced historic results at Glasgow 2026. Five women boxers won gold, and Mirabai Chanu became the first Indian weightlifter to win three consecutive Commonwealth Games gold medals. Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallists in judo, and Neeraj Chopra won silver in the men's javelin throw.
facts: Five women boxers won gold: Sakshi Chaudhary, Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Priya Ghanghas, Arundhati Choudhary
Jaismine Lamboria won the Women's 57 kg Boxing gold
Mirabai Chanu: first Indian weightlifter to win 3 consecutive CWG golds (Gold Coast 2018, Birmingham 2022, Glasgow 2026)
Judo: Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh, India's first-ever CWG gold medallists in judo
Neeraj Chopra won silver in the men's javelin throw
Neeraj Chopra returned to the Games after missing Birmingham 2022
